Chapter 2 Introduction 2.1 History of Mathematical Oncology Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells divide uncontrollably and can invade nearby tissues. Oncology is the branch of medicine concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Mathematical models can be used to study how cancer develops, grows, and spreads. By providing quantitative and predictive frameworks, mathematical models allow hypotheses about cancer to be tested and evaluated. A carcinogen is any substance that causes cancer. Carcinogenesis is the process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells. A key observation that motivated many mathematical models of carcinogenesis is cancer incidence. Cancer incidence often increases rapidly with age, while the occurrence of cancer in an individual appears highly stochastic. However, patterns emerge when cancer incidence is examined across populations. These observations contributed to the development of multistage theories of carcinogenesis, which describe cancer development as a sequence of stages or changes in cells. Beginning in the 1920s, experiments involving chemical carcinogens provided evidence for the idea that cancer develops through multiple stages. In particular, applying two different carcinogens in sequence often produced higher cancer rates than applying a single carcinogen over time, leading to the two-stage model of carcinogenesis. Charles and Luce-Clausen developed one of the first quantitative multistage theories in the 1940s, using a mathematical model to describe the development of skin tumors in mice. Their work demonstrated how mathematical models could be used to connect assumptions about cellular changes with observed cancer incidence. Armitage and Doll further developed multistage theory in the 1950s, introducing more general mathematical models that allowed different rates for different stages and treated the stages as sequential cellular changes rather than necessarily genetic mutations. Their work helped establish mathematical modelling as a framework for studying the development of cancer. 2.2 What is a Mathematical Model? A mathematical model is a numerical representation of a real-world problem. By replacing physical experimentation with mathematical simulations, it allows researchers to evaluate system dynamics and predict future outcomes. 2.3 Systems of ODEs as Mathematical Models A system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is a set of equations that involves two or more dependent variables that depend on one independent variable. A solution to this system is a set of functions that satisfies each equation on some interval \(I\). A system of ODEs can serve as a mathematical model by describing real world systems where multiple interacting components evolve over a shared independent variable. For example, in ecology, the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model uses a system of two coupled ODEs to track the interdependent population sizes of two interacting species over time \(t\). Many mathematical models are described using systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It is useful to identify equilibrium points of a system of ODEs and study the stability of the equilibria. Consider the following system of ODEs: \[ rac{dx}{dt} = f(x,y)\] \[ rac{dy}{dt} = g(x,y)\] 2.4 Review of Mathematical Concepts 2.4.1 The Characteristic Equation For a square matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n 	imes n}\), the characteristic equation is given by \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\). This yields an \(n\)-degree polynomial whose roots correspond directly to the matrix’s eigenvalues \(\lambda\). 2.4.2 The Jacobian Matrix For a vector-valued function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^m\) given by \(f(x) = (f_1(x), \dots, f_m(x))\) where \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), the Jacobian matrix \(J\) is the \(m 	imes n\) matrix of first-order partial derivatives: \[J =  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}\] When \(m=n\), i.e., the matrix is square, its determinant, commonly referred to as the Jacobian, acts as a local scaling factor. The Jacobian plays an essential role in coordinate transformations by describing how areas or volumes stretch, rotate, and distort under a change of variables. Consider the system of ODEs above. The Jacobian matrix of the system is \[J(x,y)=  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}\] This matrix contains the first order partial derivatives of \(f\) and \(g\), describing how small changes in \(x\) and \(y\) affect the rate of change of the system. 2.4.3 Equilibrium Points and Local Stability An equilibrium point is a point \((x^*, y^*)\) such that \( rac{dx}{dt} = 0\) and \( rac{dy}{dt} = 0\). That is, an equilibrium point is a point at which both variables \(x\) and \(y\) remain constant over time. At an equilibrium, there is no net change in either variable. It is important to note that the equilibrium of a system does not mean that individual processes affecting \(x\) and \(y\) have stopped. Rather, the processes are balancing each other. Finding an equilibrium tells us where a system can remain unchanged, but does not tell us what happens if the system is slightly disturbed. Stability describes how a system behaves following a small deviation from an equilibrium. An equilibrium is stable if solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close to it. An equilibrium is asymptotically stable, if it is stable and solutions that start sufficiently close will eventually approach the equilibrium. An equilibrium is unstable if it is not stable. To study the local stability of an equilibrium \((x^*, y^*)\), we analyse the eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\). Let \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) be eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\), and \((x^*, y^*)\) an equilibrium point. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and negative, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and positive, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda _ 1 < 0\) and \(\lambda_2 > 0\), with both being real, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is called a saddle point and is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with negative real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with positive real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both purely imaginary, then the linearized system exhibits oscillatory behaviour. Further analysis is required to determine stability. Zero eigenvalues require further analysis to determine stability. 2.5 Illustrative Example Consider the following model, describing a simple tumour-immune interaction based on the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey equations. Firstly, the activation term \(\alpha\) is simplistic and does not capture the complexities of immune responses to tumour growth. We also assumed proportional growth and decay, which is not realistic. Secondly, consider the case where there are no tumour cells (\(T=0\)). By (2.2), \( rac{dE}{dt}=-\delta E\). We get that \(E(t)= E(0)e^{-\delta t}\), implying that density of effector cells tends to zero over time. This is unrealistic, as effector cells are constantly present throughout the body. Thirdly, we are not modelling many factors that are involved in these tumour-effector cell interactions. This includes different tumour cell types, different effector cell types, and damage to healthy cells. Overall, this model simply demonstrates how a system of ordinary differential equations could be used to study tumour cell and effector cell interactions despite its limitations. We will gradually introduce more sophisticated models throughout the text, leading to more realistic models and useful interpretations.
